entries.meaning: A living thing that grows in soil and usually has leaves and roots. ---
examples: I killed every plant I owned until somebody gave me a pothos.
She waters the plants on Sunday mornings.
That plant needs a lot more light than it's getting.

entries.meaning: A tall plant with a woody trunk and branches. ---
examples: There's a huge oak tree in the front yard.
They planted two trees the year their daughter was born.
The storm knocked a tree down across the road.

entries.meaning: The colored part of a plant that produces seeds. ---
examples: He brought her flowers for no particular reason.
That flower only opens at night.
The flowers on the porch are starting to wilt.

entries.meaning: A part of a tree that grows out from the trunk. ---
examples: A branch came down on the power line.
The kids climbed out onto the low branches.
Trim that branch before it starts hitting the roof.

entries.meaning: A very small thin branch. ---
examples: The fire caught fast once he added some dry twigs.
A bird was carrying a twig up to its nest.
She snapped a twig off and chewed on the end of it.

entries.meaning: A small swelling on a plant that will open into a leaf or flower. ---
examples: The buds are already showing on the lilac.
Don't pick it while it's still a bud.
Warm weather brought the buds out early this year.

entries.meaning: A flower on a fruit tree or bush. ---
examples: The cherry blossoms only last about a week.
A late frost killed every blossom on the apple tree.
White blossoms covered the whole hillside.

entries.meaning: A flower, especially on a plant grown for its flowers. ---
examples: The roses put out huge blooms in June.
One bloom opened overnight.
She cut a few blooms for the table.

entries.meaning: One of the colored parts that make up a flower. ---
examples: The petals fell all over the counter.
He pulled one petal off at a time.
Rain knocked the petals off the tulips.

entries.meaning: The sweet liquid inside flowers that insects and birds feed on. ---
examples: Hummingbirds drink the nectar out of those red flowers.
We fill the feeder with sugar water instead of real nectar.
Bees turn nectar into honey.

entries.meaning: A very young plant grown from a seed. ---
examples: The tomato seedlings are ready to go outside.
Don't let a seedling dry out.
He started the seedlings under a lamp in February.

entries.meaning: A young tree with a thin trunk. ---
examples: The deer keep eating our saplings.
He staked the sapling so the wind wouldn't take it.
A row of saplings runs along the fence.

entries.meaning: The liquid that carries water and food through a plant or tree. ---
examples: Maple sap boils down into syrup.
There's sap all over the windshield.
Pine sap is almost impossible to get off your hands.

entries.meaning: A sharp point growing on the stem of a plant. ---
examples: Watch the thorns when you're cutting roses.
A thorn went straight through my glove.
He stripped the thorns off before he wrapped them.

entries.meaning: The short part of a trunk left in the ground after a tree is cut down. ---
examples: We're still trying to get that stump out.
He sat down on a stump to rest.
There are three stumps left from the old orchard.

entries.meaning: A thick piece of a tree trunk or branch that has been cut. ---
examples: Throw another log on the fire.
We split logs all afternoon.
A rotten log was blocking the trail.

entries.meaning: The hard scaly seed case of a pine tree. ---
examples: The kids filled a whole bucket with pinecones.
She glued a pinecone onto the wreath.
Pinecones crunched under the tires.

entries.meaning: The leaves of a plant or tree taken together. ---
examples: People drive up here just for the fall foliage.
Thick foliage hid the house from the road.
Cut the foliage back once it turns yellow.

entries.meaning: The layer of leaves and branches formed by the tops of trees. ---
examples: Almost no light gets through the canopy.
Monkeys spend their whole lives up in the canopy.
A hole opened in the canopy where the tree came down.

entries.meaning: A climbing evergreen plant with dark shiny leaves. ---
examples: Ivy covers the north wall of the building.
Pull the ivy off before it gets into the mortar.
There's poison ivy right where the trail starts.

entries.meaning: A plant with long feathery leaves and no flowers. ---
examples: A big fern hangs on the porch all summer.
Ferns grow thick along the creek.
That fern wants humidity, not sun.

entries.meaning: A wild plant growing somewhere it isn't wanted. ---
examples: The weeds were back within a week.
I pulled one weed and found twenty more under it.
Nothing kills those weeds for good.

entries.meaning: A woody plant smaller than a tree, with several stems coming from the ground. ---
examples: They planted low shrubs along the walkway.
That shrub needs a hard trim in the spring.
Deer will eat any shrub you put in.

entries.meaning: A tree or bush that keeps its leaves or needles all year. ---
examples: A line of evergreens blocks the wind off the field.
We planted an evergreen where the maple used to be.
The evergreens look the same in January as they do in July.

entries.meaning: Someone who takes care of a garden, for pay or as a hobby. ---
examples: My grandmother was a serious gardener.
They hired a gardener to redo the beds out front.
Gardeners around here start their seeds in March.

entries.meaning: The activity of growing and looking after plants in a garden. ---
examples: Gardening is the only thing that gets him outside.
She took up gardening after she retired.
There's a whole shelf of gardening books in the kitchen.

entries.meaning: The work of designing and planting the grounds around a building. ---
examples: The landscaping out front needs to be redone.
They spent more on landscaping than on the deck.
Good landscaping adds real value to a house.

entries.meaning: A plant grown indoors in a pot. ---
examples: She has forty houseplants in a one-bedroom apartment.
A snake plant is the easiest houseplant there is.
My houseplants barely survived the move.

entries.meaning: A plant with thick fleshy leaves that store water. ---
examples: Succulents die faster from too much water than from too little.
He keeps a row of succulents on the windowsill.
That little succulent hasn't grown in two years.

entries.meaning: A container, usually round, for growing a plant in. ---
examples: The flowerpot cracked over the winter.
There are empty flowerpots stacked up behind the shed.
Put a saucer under that flowerpot.

entries.meaning: An area of ground prepared for growing flowers. ---
examples: He edged the flower bed with brick.
Weeds took over the flower beds while we were away.
There's a narrow flower bed along the front walk.

entries.meaning: Decayed plant material added to soil to feed plants. ---
examples: We keep a bucket of scraps for the compost.
Mix a few inches of compost into each bed.
Good compost smells like a forest floor.

entries.meaning: A substance added to soil to help plants grow. ---
examples: Don't put fertilizer down right before a storm.
He uses a slow-release fertilizer in the spring.
Cheap fertilizers can burn the roots.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
entries.contrast: American fertilizer, British fertiliser — same word, different spelling.

entries.meaning: A layer of bark, straw, or leaves spread on soil to hold in moisture. ---
examples: Put down two inches of mulch around the shrubs.
The mulch keeps the weeds down.
We get mulch by the truckload every April.

entries.meaning: Animal waste spread on land to make the soil richer. ---
examples: The whole field smelled like manure.
He works aged manure into the beds every fall.
Manure has to rot before you put it near plants.

entries.meaning: A chemical used to kill insects and other pests on plants. ---
examples: They spray pesticide on the orchard twice a season.
He won't use pesticides anywhere near the vegetables.
Some pesticides stay in the soil for years.

entries.meaning: A machine for cutting grass. ---
examples: The lawn mower won't start again.
He borrowed my lawn mower and never brought it back.
Both lawn mowers in the shed are broken.

entries.meaning: A digging tool with a flat blade, used for turning over soil. ---
examples: Turn the bed over with a spade before you plant.
A spade cuts through roots better than a shovel does.
He sharpened both spades over the winter.

entries.meaning: A tool with a flat blade on a long handle, used for breaking soil and cutting weeds. ---
examples: Take a hoe down the rows and knock the weeds out.
The hoe is a lot faster than pulling them by hand.
Both hoes need new handles.

entries.meaning: A small hand tool with a curved blade for digging in a garden. ---
examples: She dug all the holes with a trowel.
I left the trowel out in the rain again.
You only need a trowel for something that small.

entries.meaning: A device that sprays water over a lawn or garden. ---
examples: The sprinklers come on at five in the morning.
Move the sprinkler over to the dry patch.
Half the sprinklers are pointed at the driveway.

entries.meaning: A container with a handle and a long spout, used for watering plants. ---
examples: Fill the watering can at the spigot outside.
She keeps a small watering can under the sink.
Both watering cans are out on the porch.

entries.meaning: Dried grass used to feed animals. ---
examples: They put up enough hay to get through the winter.
The whole barn smelled like fresh hay.
He hauls hay out to the horses every morning.

entries.meaning: A tree with thin white or silver bark that peels off in strips. ---
examples: Three white birches grow by the mailbox.
The birch lost a limb in the ice storm.
You can peel birch bark off in sheets.

entries.meaning: A tree with long thin hanging branches, usually growing near water. ---
examples: A willow leans out over the pond.
Willows drink up an enormous amount of water.
They cut the willow back every couple of years.

entries.meaning: A tall shade tree with rough-edged leaves. ---
examples: Disease killed most of the elms on this street.
There used to be a huge elm on the corner.
They're planting elms downtown again.

entries.meaning: An evergreen tree with short stiff needles and hanging cones. ---
examples: A blue spruce stands at the corner of the lot.
The spruces were planted as a windbreak.
That spruce is way too big to bring inside.

entries.meaning: An evergreen tree with flat needles, often used as a Christmas tree. ---
examples: We got a Douglas fir again this year.
The firs smell strongest right after they're cut.
A fir holds its needles longer than a spruce.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like fur, the coat of an animal.

entries.meaning: A tall fast-growing tree whose leaves shake in the slightest wind. ---
examples: A line of poplars runs along the drive.
The poplar grew twenty feet in five years.
Poplars don't live all that long.
entries.contrast: Not the same word as popular (PAHP-yuh-lur) — poplar has one syllable fewer.

entries.meaning: A tree with smooth gray bark and hard pale wood. ---
examples: Somebody carved a heart into the beech.
The beeches keep their brown leaves all winter.
That's a copper beech, not a maple.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like beach, the sand by the ocean.

entries.meaning: A tree or bush with large white or pink flowers. ---
examples: The magnolia blooms before it puts out any leaves.
Magnolias grow everywhere down south.
A late frost browned every flower on the magnolia.

entries.meaning: A flower with a strong sweet scent that grows on a thorny bush. ---
examples: He sent a dozen roses to her office.
The rose by the gate blooms all summer.
Roses need a lot more water than people think.

entries.meaning: A brightly colored cup-shaped spring flower that grows from a bulb. ---
examples: The tulips came up right through the snow.
She bought a bunch of tulips at the market.
Every tulip in the bed is red except one.

entries.meaning: A small flower with white petals around a yellow center. ---
examples: Daisies grow wild along the fence.
She picked a daisy and stuck it behind her ear.
There was a jar of daisies on the kitchen table.

entries.meaning: A large flower with curved petals, grown from a bulb. ---
examples: The lilies open a few days after you cut them.
One lily can scent a whole room.
Pull the pollen out of lilies or it stains everything.

entries.meaning: A flower with unusually shaped petals, often grown indoors in a pot. ---
examples: That orchid has been alive for six years.
Orchids die from overwatering more than anything else.
He gave her an orchid instead of cut flowers.
entries.contrast: The ch is pronounced like k: OR-kid.

entries.meaning: A yellow spring flower with a trumpet-shaped center, grown from a bulb. ---
examples: Daffodils are the first thing up in March.
He planted two hundred daffodils along the drive.
The daffodil came up but never opened.

entries.meaning: A small purple or blue flower that grows low to the ground. ---
examples: Violets spread through the whole lawn.
She keeps an African violet on the windowsill.
A few violets came up between the stones.

entries.meaning: A flower with thin bright red or orange petals. ---
examples: Whole fields of poppies open in May.
A single poppy came up in the gravel.
The poppies only last a day or two.

entries.meaning: A flower with ruffled petals and a spicy smell, common in bouquets. ---
examples: They dyed the carnations blue for the dance.
Carnations last a lot longer in a vase than roses.
He wore a white carnation on his lapel.

entries.meaning: A bush with clusters of small purple or white flowers and a strong scent. ---
examples: The lilac by the back door blooms for about two weeks.
You can smell the lilacs from the street.
She cut an armful of lilac for the table.

entries.meaning: A low bush with narrow gray-green leaves and fragrant purple flowers. ---
examples: There's lavender planted all along the walk.
She dries lavender and puts it in the drawers.
Bees are all over the lavender in July.

entries.meaning: A common weed with a yellow flower that turns into a ball of white seeds. ---
examples: The whole yard is dandelions by the middle of May.
He blew the seeds off a dandelion.
You can eat dandelion greens in a salad.

entries.meaning: A low plant with three round leaves on each stem, common in lawns. ---
examples: There's more clover in the lawn than grass.
She spent an hour looking for a four-leaf clover.
Bees work the clover all afternoon.
entries.contrast: Don't confuse clover (the plant) with clove (the spice, or a piece of garlic).

entries.meaning: A flower that grows on its own, without being planted. ---
examples: The wildflowers along the highway are seeded on purpose.
We hiked up to see the wildflowers in June.
He couldn't name a single wildflower.

entries.meaning: A round full flower that blooms in the fall. ---
examples: Every porch on the block has chrysanthemums in October.
She bought one chrysanthemum in a pot.
The chrysanthemums held up through the first frost.
entries.contrast: The ch is pronounced like k, and the stress falls on the second syllable: krih-SAN-thuh-muhm.

entries.meaning: A bunch of flowers arranged and tied together. ---
examples: She caught the bouquet at the wedding.
He showed up with a bouquet and an apology.
They deliver bouquets the same day.
entries.contrast: The t is silent and the stress is on the second syllable: boh-KAY.

entries.meaning: A ring of leaves or flowers used as a decoration.
examples: There's a wreath on every door on the street.
She made the wreath out of pine and holly.
The wreaths go up right after Thanksgiving.
entries.contrast: The w is silent: REETH. The plural is voiced, REETHZ.
